5.3.1. A Boolean Result Answers a Question #

5.3.1. A Boolean Result Answers a Question # A returned result need not be a number to print. A method can answer a question, and a bool result can become the condition of an if statement. Suppose an order receives free delivery when its subtotal is at least 50. The question is whether an order qualifies, not how much its delivery costs. Keeping those contracts distinct helps explain why two related methods may have different return types. Trace the boundary: 49.99 does not qualify, 50 qualifies, and 50.01 qualifies. The equality is part of the rule. Writing > instead of >= would still compile and would pass examples far from the threshold. T

15.1.6. A Complete Generic Array Stack # Chapter 14’s dynamic array becomes a stack by exposing only the final live slot. 14.2.9. A Complete Singly Linked Sequence #

14.2.9. A Complete Singly Linked Sequence # This wrapper presents the same Add , Insert , indexer, and RemoveAt operations as the dynamic array. Nodes are private so client code cannot accidentally create cycles or change count without updating the wrapper. NodeAt validates the index, then follows links. head! and Next! express facts established by the list invariants after validation; they do not create runtime null checks. If those invariants are broken, the suppression cannot repair them. Run the cell independently. It inserts the middle order, removes the head, empties the list, and appends again. The last line should be count=1, first=WO

20.2.5. A Protected Route Graph # Encapsulation should protect graph rules, not merely hide a field’s name. RouteGraph uses private neighbor dictionaries and returns copied arrays for vertices and neighbors. A caller can edit its copy without changing the stored graph. Returning a mutable collection as IEnumerable would not protect it: a caller could cast it back to the original collection type. The contract requires explicit vertices. SetEdge checks both endpoints and weight rules before changing either direction. A new logical edge increases EdgeCount once; replacing its weight changes both reciprocal entries without changing EdgeCount. Try

5.1.2. A Repeated Task Needs a Name #

5.1.2. A Repeated Task Needs a Name # A shop prints a store name and separator on every receipt. Copying those two statements for every receipt works at first, but a store-name change must then be made in several places. A method names the task once so callers can reuse it. This is decomposition : divide a larger program into understandable responsibilities. Before refactoring, the statements appear twice: print store name print separator print store name print separator After refactoring, two calls use one definition. Predict the output: defining the helper does not print anything by itself. 1 using System ; 2 3 PrintHeader (); 4 PrintHeader

5.1.1.4. A Small Schema #

5.1.1.4. A Small Schema # A schema is the planned structure of a database. Here is a small bookstore schema: CREATE TABLE Books ( BookId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , Title TEXT NOT NULL , Author TEXT NOT NULL , Price REAL NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Sales ( SaleId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , BookId INTEGER NOT NULL , Quantity INTEGER NOT NULL , SoldOn TEXT NOT NULL , FOREIGN KEY ( BookId ) REFERENCES Books ( BookId ) ); Books stores facts about each book. Sales stores events that happened over time. The foreign key tells us which book each sale refers to.

17.2.1. A Visit and a Returned Result Are Different Events # A traversal chooses when to visit a node relative to its children. Preorder visits B, A, C; inorder visits A, B, C; postorder visits A, C, B. These names describe timing, not three different storage layouts. The same nodes and edges support all three orders. abstract data type

Replaced with the listed canonical subject terms at the preserved teaching locations.
13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies #

13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies # An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does not require one particular internal representation. For a stack, the contract might say: Operation Meaning Push(item) Add an item to the top. Pop() Remove and return the top item. Peek() Return the top item without removing it. Count Report how many items are stored. This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

13. ADTs #

13. ADTs # This chapter covers abstract data types, interfaces, invariants, references, operation costs, and generic implementations. The short name ADTs keeps the sidebar compact, but the full scope is about separating what a data structure promises from how it is represented in memory. Abstract data type : An ADT specifies values and operations separately from implementation details. Interface : An interface names the operations a type promises to provide. 3.9.3. Designing for Everyone #

3.9.3. Designing for Everyone # Software that only works for some people quietly excludes the rest. Accessibility means designing software that people with disabilities can use, for example with a screen reader or without a mouse. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.2, a W3C Recommendation first published in October 2023) organize accessibility around four principles: content must be perceivable , operable , understandable , and robust . [ 3 ] Even a console program can follow these principles. Do not let color carry meaning by itself; say it in words: 1 using System ; 2 3 // Status messages that do not depend on color alone. 4 /

Accessing Array Elements # The elements inside an array can to referenced with the same index notation used earlier for strings. a[2] refers to the element at index 2 (third element because of 0 based indexing). Unlike with strings, this element can not only be read, but also be assigned to: a[0] = 7; a[1] = 5; a[2] = 9; a[3] = 6; These four assignment statements would replace the original 0 values for each element in the array. This is a verbose way to specify all array values. An array with the same final data could be created with the single declaration: int[] b = {7, 5, 9, 6}; Fig. 7.2 New array initialized with braces. # The list

21.3.1. Account for the Children and the Work Around Them #

21.3.1. Account for the Children and the Work Around Them # A recurrence models the work of a recursive algorithm. It is not the algorithm’s return-value equation unless the counted work happens to satisfy the same relation. A recursive sum may return a monetary total while its call count follows a completely different equation. Name the quantity being modeled and include the base cost. For a one-step reduction, suppose C(0)=1 and C(n)=1+C(n-1). Unfolding gives C(n)=1+1+C(n-2), then n non-base contributions plus the base contribution. Thus C(n)=n+1 under this counting convention. Omitting the base call changes exact counts but not linear grow

20.2.3. Adjacency Collections #

20.2.3. Adjacency Collections # An adjacency list stores each vertex’s actual neighbors. The term includes several concrete choices: a list, a set, or a dictionary of neighbor-to-weight pairs. These choices have different lookup and update costs. A list supports neighbor iteration but must scan to find a particular neighbor, and it can contain duplicates unless insertion checks for them. A hash set supports expected constant-time membership for unweighted edges. A neighbor dictionary supports expected constant-time lookup and weight replacement while keeping one entry per neighbor. All retain explicit entries for isolated vertices. 1 using Sy

20.2.1. Adjacency Matrices #

20.2.1. Adjacency Matrices # An adjacency matrix reserves one cell for each ordered pair of vertices. A row describes outgoing connections from its vertex; a column describes incoming connections to its vertex. Map symbolic labels to dense integer indexes before accessing the array. For the six-room undirected graph, a Boolean matrix has 36 cells, although only eight are true. Four logical edges appear twice, once in each direction. Its diagonal is false because the model rejects self-loops. An isolated vertex still has a row and column, both empty. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Generic ; 3 using System.Linq ; 4 5 string [] room

Why Coding When AI Writes Code #

Why Coding When AI Writes Code # AI assistants now generate working code from a short description. That makes the skills in this book more important, not less. Someone still has to state precisely what a program should do, decides whether the code an assistant produces is correct, work with the agents to make sure the development is in the right direction, and judge which tradeoffs make better sense. Those are the skills this book practices. 14.1.9. Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost #

14.1.9. Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost # For nine appends, the trace copies 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends. For a longer sequence, copy sizes form 2 + 4 + 8 + ... . Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. Adding one write per appended item still gives a total proportional to n . Dividing total work by n gives a constant amortized cost. This is a bound over an operation sequence, n

14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing #

14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing # Dynamic arrays have two different stories: Reading items[index] is O(1) because the index points directly to the slot. Most appends are O(1), but an append that triggers resizing is O(n) because it copies existing values. Over many appends, doubling capacity gives amortized O(1) append cost. Amortized means the occasional expensive resize is spread across many cheap operations.

An important subtlety in C# is integer division : when both operands are int , the / operator truncates toward zero and discards any remainder. To get a decimal result, at least one operand must be a double (or another floating-point type): 10 / 3 ; // → 3 (integer division, remainder discarded) 10.0 / 3 ; // → 3.333... (double division) 10 % 3 ; // → 1 (remainder)

7. Arrays #

7. Arrays # An array is a collection type : it groups a fixed number of elements of one type and lets the program access them by position. A collection is the broader idea of grouping values and providing operations for working with them. Arrays are the first collection family we study in detail. This chapter covers one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, including declaration, initialization, traversal, and method use. Array : An array stores a fixed number of same-typed values under one name. Index : An index selects a specific element by position. Traversal : Loops let a program visit each array element systematically. Two-dimensional

13.2.6. Counting Work and Big-O #

13.2.6. Counting Work and Big-O # Let n be the number of records. Count a representative operation before comparing implementations. Big-O describes an upper bound on how work grows with input size, ignoring fixed factors for sufficiently large inputs. It is not an elapsed time or automatically a worst-case claim. Bound Example Effect of doubling input O(1) Reading one array slot Bounded work independent of size. O(log n) Repeatedly halving a search interval About one extra halving. O(n) Scanning all records About twice the work. O(n log n) A typical comparison sort Slightly more than twice the work. O(n²) Comparing every pair About four time

13.2.7. Operation Costs #

13.2.7. Operation Costs # A data structure is not just correct or incorrect. It also has costs. Operation Array/List-backed stack Linked-node stack Push Usually O(1); occasional resize costs O(n) O(1) Pop O(1) O(1) Peek O(1) O(1) Random access by index O(1), if exposed O(n) Extra memory per item low one extra reference per node The best representation depends on the workload. If a program mostly pushes and pops at one end, either representation can work. If it needs fast index access, linked nodes are the wrong fit.

1.1.5. Number Systems and Data Representation # A binary , or base-2, number uses the digits 0 and 1 . Each position has a value that is a power of two, just as decimal positions represent powers of ten. A byte contains eight bits, so it has 2^8 = 256 possible patterns, from 0000 0000 through 1111 1111 . The ASCII code for uppercase A is decimal 65. Its eight-bit representation is 0100 0001 . Work from right to left to convert the pattern: Bit position 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 Place value 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 Bit in 0100 0001 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 Only the 64 and 1 positions are set, so the value is 64 + 1 = 65 . 17.4.2. Range Queries and Pruning #

17.4.2. Range Queries and Pruning # Suppose staff want all active IDs from 25 through 60, inclusive. One method gets every ID and filters the resulting list. A BST can also skip subtrees that cannot contain a match. Pruning means using a proved constraint to avoid visiting part of a structure. At key 20, the entire left subtree is below the lower bound 25. At key 60, the entire right subtree is above the upper bound 60. For keys within the interval, process left, node, and right to keep the result ordered. Bounds are inclusive for the query even though the BST’s ordering invariant is strict. 1.3.7. Blocks, Formatting, and Comments #

1.3.7. Blocks, Formatting, and Comments # A block groups code between curly braces, { and } . In the complete program, one pair encloses the class body and another encloses the Main body. Indent the statements inside each block so readers can see the nesting. Braces define that structure for C#; indentation makes it visible. Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and line breaks. Outside quoted text, extra whitespace often changes readability without changing behavior. You still need separation between words such as class and Program . 3.1.2. Boolean Data Type #

3.1.2. Boolean Data Type # The condition in an if statement is a Boolean expression — also called a relational expression . Every expression in C# produces a value, and the defining feature of a Boolean expression is that its value is always either true or false (think: Yes/No, On/Off, 1/0). This two-state result is represented by C#’s bool type, whose only legal values are true and false . You can quickly try bool variables with csharprepl , Run C# , or a small VS Code project: > bool isRollaQuiet = true; > bool isChicagoClose = false; > isRollaQuiet true > isChicagoClose false The same Boolean values work directly in a console program. 5.5.5. Bounded Extensions: Overloading and Recursion #

5.5.5. Bounded Extensions: Overloading and Recursion # These are recognition-level extensions, not prerequisites for the required method tasks. In a class, overloading permits the same member name with distinct parameter signatures; changing only the return type does not create a distinct overload. Local functions in the same local scope cannot be overloaded this way. Recursion means a method calls itself; it needs a termination policy and is developed with later data-structure/algorithm lessons. The preview’s extension items and the original homework research questions should not be used to assess untaught core skills. Footnotes [ 1 ] Furthe

4.1.3. break and continue #

4.1.3. break and continue # break exits the nearest loop or switch. continue skips the rest of the current loop body. In a for loop, the update runs before the next condition check; in a while loop, the next condition is checked directly. Ensure an update is not skipped accidentally. return exits a method and is taught with user-defined methods in Chapter 5. It is not needed for this chapter’s programs.

26.2.1. Build the Fallback Table Before Scanning Text # KMP avoids restarting a search from scratch after every mismatch. It retains a fact already proved: a suffix of the consumed text matches a prefix of the pattern. This connects direct matching’s result contract to a different reuse rule. The goal remains all overlapping ordinal matches; changing the algorithm must not change that answer. For each pattern position i, prefix[i] records the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix. Proper excludes the entire segment. The number is a length, not an index of the next text character. For ABABACA, complete the table from l

2.2.4. Keep Stored Values Separate from Their Display #

2.2.4. Keep Stored Values Separate from Their Display # Formatting a price to two places produces text for a report. It does not change the stored price into a two-decimal business amount. Likewise, a value displayed as 0.33 might come from several more precise internal values. Decide where a rounding rule belongs and state it explicitly. Use decimal for the chapter’s straightforward decimal-price arithmetic, while recognizing that currency rules involve more than choosing that type. Guided check: a badge code is "0042" . Would converting it to an integer preserve its identifying representation? Would it help calculate how many badges exist?

Why C# #

Why C# # C# is a general-purpose, statically typed language at the center of Microsoft’s open-source, cross-platform .NET platform. It is a good first language for this book for four reasons: Types are visible. Every variable has a declared type that the compiler checks before the program runs. Beginners see how data is represented, and many mistakes are caught as compile errors instead of surprising results. It is used where business software is built. C# and .NET power enterprise web services, internal business applications, cloud back ends, and database-driven systems, the same kind of information systems this book builds toward. It is fre

12.4.5. Calling base and Sealing an Override #

12.4.5. Calling base and Sealing an Override # A class inherits directly from one base class and can implement multiple interfaces. A virtual base method permits an override with a matching signature. A derived implementation may call base.Draw() to preserve the base action and then extend it. Use sealed override to close one virtual member to further overriding while still permitting inheritance from the class. This differs from a sealed class, which cannot be inherited at all. In the original shape example, Rectangle seals Draw. Square may derive from Rectangle and inherits that implementation, but it cannot override Draw again. [ 3 ] Predi

14.1.2. Resizing by Copying #

14.1.2. Resizing by Copying # When the array fills up, the dynamic array cannot stretch the existing array. It allocates a larger array, copies the existing values, then continues adding into the new storage. A common strategy is to double the capacity each time resizing is needed. This makes individual resize steps expensive, but keeps most Add operations cheap. 1 static int [] Grow ( int [] oldStorage ) 2 { 3 int [] larger = new int [ oldStorage . How Each Chapter Works #

How Each Chapter Works # Each chapter is one week of work. A chapter opens with a landing page that lists its sections, followed by content sections, usually three, each sized for one class meeting. The first section introduces the chapter’s main ideas, and the later sections each take one focused topic. Every section includes code you can run and modify. 8. Data Collections #

8. Data Collections # Arrays are the first collection type we studied in Chapter 7 . This chapter expands our choices. Collections organize groups of values and define how programs work with them; arrays remain part of that broader category. We first compare the major .NET collection families and their access patterns, then develop lists and dictionaries as practical tools for everyday programs. Collection families : Arrays, lists, linked lists, dictionaries, sets, stacks, queues, and priority queues provide different access rules. List : A List<T> stores an ordered sequence that can grow or shrink. Dictionary : A Dictionary<TKey, TValue> map

Indent the statements inside each block so readers can see the nesting. Braces define that structure for C#; indentation makes it visible. Whitespace includes spaces, tabs, and line breaks. Outside quoted text, extra whitespace often changes readability without changing behavior. You still need separation between words such as class and Program . 2.2.1.2. Common Data Types in C# # C# is a “strongly typed” language, meaning that every variable and constant has a type. In addition to variables, types are also required for expressions that evaluate to a value, method declarations with names, input parameters, and return values. 23.2.1. Compare the Invariant That Each Sort Maintains # Selection sort, insertion sort and bubble sort can all order the same small invoice array, but they establish progress differently. 12.4.1.1. Compare the Three Styles #

12.4.1.1. Compare the Three Styles # In a procedural design, a function can receive an order total and calculate a result. In an object-oriented design, an object can own validated order state and expose the needed behavior. In a functional style, a calculation can return a result from supplied values without modifying shared state. C# supports combining these styles; choosing classes does not make every design object-oriented or eliminate the need for functions. For a receipt system, separate the calculation from console formatting and file storage. State which concern each component handles and how you can test calculation without printing

In an object-oriented design, an object can own validated order state and expose the needed behavior. In a functional style, a calculation can return a result from supplied values without modifying shared state. C# supports combining these styles; choosing classes does not make every design object-oriented or eliminate the need for functions. 25.1.1. Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule # A repeated subproblem is a question with the same complete state, not just a similarly named function call. Changing the base values creates a different sequence and invalidates an old cache. For F(4), the naive call tree asks for F(3) and F(2). F(3) asks for F(2) and F(1), so F(2) is expanded twice. 2.3.1.3. Comparison Operators #

2.3.1.3. Comparison Operators # Comparison operators (also called relational operators ) compare two values and always return a bool — either true or false . They are the primary building blocks of conditions in if statements and loops: int a = 5 , b = 3 ; a == b ; // false — equality (note: two equals signs, not one) a != b ; // true — not equal a > b ; // true — greater than A very common bug is writing = (assignment) instead of == (equality test) inside a condition. C# will often catch this as a compile-time error.

Computers encode data as bits, each with two possible values, conventionally written 0 and 1 . Eight bits form a byte. An encoding determines what a sequence of bits means: a number, text, an image, or another kind of data. The same bit pattern can mean different things under different encodings. 2.4.3. Output # In a regular C# program, including the VS Code projects used in this book, values are not displayed just because an expression exists in the source code. You must explicitly give the program an instruction to print to the console or terminal. This printing is accomplished through a method with a long name: Console.WriteLine . Like with math, you can pass a method a value to work on, by placing it in parentheses after the name of the method. Console is a C# class maintained by the system, that interacts with the terminal or console window where text output appears for the program. A method defined in that class is WriteLine . T

2.2.3. Follow a Value Through a Conversion #

2.2.3. Follow a Value Through a Conversion # Suppose three employees share ten work hours. The expression 10 / 3 has two integer operands, so it produces the integer 3. Assigning that result to a double afterward produces 3.0; the missing fractional part cannot be recovered. Converting an operand before division changes which arithmetic operation is performed. This is the same evaluation-order reasoning used for ordinary expressions: work out each intermediate value and its type before considering the destination variable. Like with math, you can pass a method a value to work on, by placing it in parentheses after the name of the method. Console is a C# class maintained by the system, that interacts with the terminal or console window where text output appears for the program. A method defined in that class is WriteLine . T

13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies #

13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies # An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does not require one particular internal representation. For a stack, the contract might say: Operation Meaning Push(item) Add an item to the top. Pop() Remove and return the top item. Peek() Return the top item without removing it. Count Report how many items are stored. This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules #

13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules # A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules: Pop removes the same item that Peek would return. Count increases after Push and decreases after Pop . Pop and Peek on an empty stack are errors. A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an invariant . Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.

15.1.7. Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations #

15.1.7. Correctness and Cost of Stack Operations # Push preserves the invariant by growing without changing count, writing to the first unused slot, and increasing count once. Pop first obtains the current top, then reduces count and clears precisely the slot that left the live range. It never shifts other values. Pop and peek take O(1) time. Push takes O(1) on most calls, O(n) when growth copies n live values, and O(1) amortized across repeated pushes using the chapter 15 doubling argument. A linked stack can push and pop at the head in O(1) link operations, but allocates a node per push. Array locality and spare capacity are different memor

14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing #

14.1.4. Cost of Append and Indexing # Dynamic arrays have two different stories: Reading items[index] is O(1) because the index points directly to the slot. Most appends are O(1), but an append that triggers resizing is O(n) because it copies existing values. Over many appends, doubling capacity gives amortized O(1) append cost. Amortized means the occasional expensive resize is spread across many cheap operations.

7.1.3. Creating Arrays #

7.1.3. Creating Arrays # A C# array variable is declared similarly to a non-array variable, with the addition of square brackets ( [] ) after the type specifier to denote it as an array. So, the general form for declaring an array variable of the element type is: type [] variableName; For example, if you want to create an array called a with the type int for elements, you declare the array variable as: int[] a; In this declaration, you do not know how many elements will be in this array from the preceding declaration. You must give further information to create the corresponding array object . A new object can be created using the new syntax.

Integer Types # Integer types store whole numbers with no fractional part. The most common choice is int (32-bit signed), which covers roughly ±2.1 billion. Default Values # Every type has a default value — the value a variable gets if C# has to fill it in without one you provided (for example, in an uninitialized array element, or a field you have not assigned in a constructor). 20.4.5. Depth-First Search and Cycles #

20.4.5. Depth-First Search and Cycles # Depth-first search (DFS) follows a branch before returning to another neighbor. Mark before following neighbors: a cycle then leads to an already visited vertex rather than infinite recursion. This teaching implementation uses recursive calls; the runtime call stack records unfinished work. It can require O(V) stack space and very deep graphs may exceed runtime stack limits. Part VII develops further traversal techniques. DFS discovers reachability, but its discovery depth does not promise a shortest route. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Generic ; 3 4 SimpleGraph graph = new SimpleGraph ();

21.1.1. Derive a Count Before Naming a Growth Class # A report compares each invoice with every later invoice. 5.1.5. Designing Methods #

5.1.5. Designing Methods # A caller needs a result without repeating the calculation. Start by stating the method’s job, input types, result type, and assumptions. Then write a definition and calls that check that contract. In this section, keep the question “what does the caller receive?” separate from “what appears on the screen?” For a simple integer square, the contract is: accept an integer in a range whose square fits in int, return its square, and print nothing inside the calculation. We use small inputs here; arbitrary large integers need a stated overflow policy.

The queue is not a list of completed rooms; it holds discovered rooms whose neighbors still need examination. 20.3.3. Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors #

20.3.3. Discover a Vertex Once, Then Process Its Neighbors # A delivery graph has edges A-B, A-C, B-D and C-D. Starting at A, how many roads are needed to reach each stop? Breadth-first search answers a minimum-hop question in an unweighted graph. It keeps a queue of discovered vertices whose outgoing neighbors still need examination. Discovery and processing are different events: a vertex can already be known while it is still waiting in the queue. Mark a vertex discovered when it is enqueued. 23.4.1. Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem #

23.4.1. Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem # Shell sort connects to insertion sort by ordering positions separated by a chosen gap. With gap three, positions zero, three, six form one subsequence; positions one, four, seven form another. A pass applies insertion-like work within each subsequence. It does not claim the whole array is already sorted after that pass. As gaps shrink, long-distance disorder can be reduced before the final gap-one insertion pass. 3.2.6. else-if Statements #

3.2.6. else-if Statements # Comparing with the if-else statement, the else if statements specify a new condition to be tested if the first condition is False. The syntax for the else-if statement is: if ( condition1 ) { // block of code to be executed if condition1 is True } else if ( condition2 ) { // block of code to be executed if the condition1 is False and condition2 is True } else { // block of code to be executed if the condition1 is False and condition2 is False } Note that the logic of the flow terminate at else : The else block is the default block when all the conditions are False. An example of else-if statement is: 1 int x = 10 ;

6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question #

6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question # Ethical decisions in software are rarely about villains. They are usually about trade-offs under deadline pressure. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped: Who is affected? List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it. What could happen, and how bad would it be? Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder. What do we owe them? Consider laws, contracts, promises made to customers, and professional codes. Could we explain this decision publicly? If a decision only works while nobody knows about it, reconsider it.

4.4.1. Euclid’s Algorithm # The greatest common divisor of two non-zero integers is a great example to illustrate the power of loops. Everyone learns about the concept of a greatest common divisor when faced with a fraction that is not in reduced form. Consider the fraction \(\frac{2}{4}\) , which is the same as \(\frac{1}{2}\) . The fraction \(\frac{2}{4}\) can be reduced, because the numerator and denominator both have greatest common factor of 2. That is, \(\frac{2}{4} = \frac{1 \cdot 2}{2 \cdot 2}\) . 19.3.5. Explain the Selection # A dynamic array supports fast indexed access and sequential reports. Linked storage makes known-node updates convenient but does not make locating a node free. Stacks and queues restrict access order. Balanced ordered collections support ordered lookup; a heap supports priority selection; a hash collection supports equality-based access. 16.1.3. First-Match Linear Search # Linear search visits values in order and returns immediately when equality succeeds. It accepts unsorted data. Return the first matching index or -1; preserve the input and do not treat index zero as a missing result. The processed prefix contains no match. 2.2.1. Types #

2.2.1. Types # In C#, everything is a type . Every value you store, every variable you declare, and every expression you write has a type. A type defines three things: Value : The set of valid values it can hold (e.g., int holds whole numbers −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647). Operation : The operations permitted on those values (e.g., arithmetic on numbers, .Length on strings). Memory : The amount of memory reserved when a variable of that type is created. C# types split into two fundamental categories: value types and reference types . The difference between them is not just a classification detail — it changes what happens when you assign o

2.2.3. Follow a Value Through a Conversion #

2.2.3. Follow a Value Through a Conversion # Suppose three employees share ten work hours. The expression 10 / 3 has two integer operands, so it produces the integer 3. Assigning that result to a double afterward produces 3.0; the missing fractional part cannot be recovered. Converting an operand before division changes which arithmetic operation is performed. This is the same evaluation-order reasoning used for ordinary expressions: work out each intermediate value and its type before considering the destination variable. 4.4.3. GCD Subtraction Method #

4.4.3. GCD Subtraction Method # The subtraction method (also attributable to Euclid) to compute the Greatest Common Divisor works as follows: Based on the mathematical definition in the previous section, the greatest common divisor algorithm saves a step when we already have a and b in the right order . The right order means that \(a > b\) . As we noted earlier, the cleverness of the mathematical definition is that a and b are swapped as the first step to ensure that \(a > b\) , after which we can repeatedly divide to get the GCD. Division, of course, is a form of repetitive subtraction, so the way to divide by b is to repeatedly subtract it

4.4.3. GCD Subtraction Method # The subtraction method (also attributable to Euclid) to compute the Greatest Common Divisor works as follows: Based on the mathematical definition in the previous section, the greatest common divisor algorithm saves a step when we already have a and b in the right order . The right order means that \(a > b\) . As we noted earlier, the cleverness of the mathematical definition is that a and b are swapped as the first step to ensure that \(a > b\) , after which we can repeatedly divide to get the GCD. Division, of course, is a form of repetitive subtraction, so the way to divide by b is to repeatedly subtract it

8.2.2. Generic Collections #

8.2.2. Generic Collections # A collection’s family tells you how it organizes access. Its element type tells you what values it stores. These are separate choices: a list of integers and a list of strings use the same sequence operations, but they store different kinds of values. A generic type is defined using one or more type parameters , which are placeholders for types. In documentation, List<T> means a list whose element type is represented by T . When you write List<string> , string is the type argument you have supplied for that parameter. The library provides the reusable class; you choose its type arguments when declaring the collect

13.3.7. Generic Interfaces #

13.3.7. Generic Interfaces # An ADT contract can be generic too. IStack<T> describes stack behavior for any element type T , while each implementation decides how to store those elements. interface IStack < T > { int Count { get ; } void Push ( T item ); T Pop (); T Peek (); } This is the same idea behind library interfaces such as IEnumerable<T> , ICollection<T> , and IList<T> : the interface names the behavior, and the type parameter names the element type.

13.3.1. Why Generics Exist #

13.3.1. Why Generics Exist # Without generics, a stack that holds int would need to be a different class from a stack that holds string , or it would have to store everything as object and lose type safety. Generics let one implementation work for many types: // Non-generic — stores object, loses type safety var list = new ArrayList (); list . Add ( 1 ); list . Add ( "oops" ); // compiles — bug at runtime // Generic — type-safe at compile time var nums = new List < int > (); nums . Add ( 1 ); // nums.Add("oops"); // compile error For related explanation, see the further reading below. [ 1 ]

RouteGraph uses private neighbor dictionaries and returns copied arrays for vertices and neighbors. A caller can edit its copy without changing the stored graph. Following those predecessor links backward reconstructs a route to the source. Reverse the route to display it from source to destination. The source is a one-vertex route to itself; an unreachable known vertex has no source route. Do not fabricate a destination-only path when no predecessor chain exists. Why is the distance minimal? 15.2.9. Growing a Ring and Choosing a Deque Representation # A growable ring allocates a larger array when full. Copy logical item i from (front + i) % oldCapacity into new slot i, then set front to zero. Count stays unchanged; the next insertion slot becomes count. For the full layout [E, B, C, D] with front one, growth must produce [B, C, D, E, unused, ...] , not [E, B, C, D, ...] . The bounded ring above has O(1) worst-case operation work and no growth. WriteLine ( $"n={n}, calls={HalvingCalls(n)}" ); 6 int HalvingCalls ( int size ) 7 { 8 if ( size < 0 ) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException ( nameof ( size )); 9 return size <= 1 ? 1 : 1 + HalvingCalls ( size / 2 ); 10 } For powers of two, the chain is n, n/2, …, 1. For n=9 the integer chain is 9,4,2,1. Depth and time are Θ(log n) for large n; zero

1.2.3. Handle Personal Information with Care #

1.2.3. Handle Personal Information with Care # Personal data identifies a person or can be connected to one. Names and contact details are familiar examples. Purchase history, borrowing history, and account activity can also describe someone when linked to an identifier. Replacing a name with a customer number does not necessarily make a record anonymous: another record may connect the number to the person. Privacy concerns appropriate collection, use, sharing, and retention of information about people. Security concerns protecting information and systems from unauthorized access or changes and keeping services available. The concerns overlap

1.1.1. Computers, Software, and Data #

1.1.1. Computers, Software, and Data # Hardware is the physical equipment, including a processor, memory, storage, and input/output devices. Software supplies instructions. An operating system manages hardware and provides services to applications, such as reading a file or displaying text. Computers encode data as bits, each with two possible values, conventionally written 0 and 1 . Eight bits form a byte. An encoding determines what a sequence of bits means: a number, text, an image, or another kind of data. The same bit pattern can mean different things under different encodings. You will choose C# data types in Chapter 2; a type constrain

11.3.2. Has-a Relationships #

11.3.2. Has-a Relationships # Composition builds a larger object from smaller objects. An order has lines; a line refers to a product. In contrast, an order is not a product. Inheritance would make the wrong promise in that relationship. The term aggregation is sometimes used for a looser relationship in which an object refers to independently managed objects. In this design the order creates its lines, while several lines can share a product created by client code. State the actual ownership and sharing rules rather than relying on the terminology alone. Type Responsibility Information it needs Product Describe one catalog version. SKU, name

18.1.3. Heap Representation # A heap is a common priority-queue representation. A binary heap has two key rules: Shape rule : the tree is complete, filled level by level from left to right. Order rule : in a min-heap, each parent priority is less than or equal to its child priorities. Because the shape is complete, a heap can be stored compactly in an array. 1.3.5. Names, Keywords, and Case # An identifier names something in a program, such as Program or Main . C# is case-sensitive : Console , console , and CONSOLE are different spellings. Library names must match their declarations exactly, so use Console.WriteLine , including the capital C , W , and L . A keyword has a language-defined role. Reserved keywords , such as class , static , and void , are reserved for the language itself and cannot be ordinary identifiers. You have already seen them in the first console program; do not replace them with names of your own. Ordinary identifiers begin with a letter or underscore and can include digits

1.2.1. Identify Stakeholders and Possible Harm # A stakeholder is a person or group affected by a system or a decision about it. In a bookstore, a cashier uses the sales system, a customer relies on its receipt, a manager uses its reports, and warehouse staff act on its stock requests. 13.4.1. Why foreach Works # foreach is not built-in magic tied to List<T> or Dictionary<TKey, TValue> specifically. GetEnumerator ()

16.2.3. Insert into a Sorted Prefix #

16.2.3. Insert into a Sorted Prefix # At the start of iteration i, positions zero through i-1 are sorted and contain the same occurrences as before. Save values[i] before shifting anything. Move larger prefix values one position to the right, then store the saved value in the gap. For [30,10,20], insert 10 into [30] to obtain [10,30,20]. Then save 20, shift 30, and place 20 between 10 and 30. The array is never extended or shortened. The saved current value prevents shifts from overwriting the item being inserted. Pass Sorted prefix afterward Remaining values Start 30 10, 20 Insert 10 10, 30 20 Insert 20 10, 20, 30 None Use a strict greater-t

2.2.1.3.1. Integer Types #

2.2.1.3.1. Integer Types # Integer types store whole numbers with no fractional part. The most common choice is int (32-bit signed), which covers roughly ±2.1 billion. Use long (64-bit) when you need a larger range, or byte for small non-negative values (0–255). Unsigned variants ( uint , ulong , ushort , byte ) hold only non-negative values, which doubles the positive range but disallows negatives. Numeric literals default to int . Use suffixes to specify other types: L / l for long , U / u for uint , UL / ul for ulong . 1 int population = 2 _147_483_647 ; // int max (~2.1 billion); _ is a digit separator 2 long worldPopulation = 8 _000_000_

3.9.1. Who Owns Code #

3.9.1. Who Owns Code # Code is a creative work, so copyright protects it automatically: you may not copy someone else’s code just because you can see it. A license is the owner’s permission to use the code under stated terms. Two common open-source examples: The MIT License is permissive : anyone may use, copy, modify, and sell the code, as long as they keep the copyright and license notice. [ 1 ] The GNU General Public License (GPL) is copyleft : if you distribute a modified version, you must release it under the GPL as well. [ 2 ] Code written for an employer usually belongs to the employer. Code with no license at all is not free to reuse.

13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules #

13.1.6. Contracts Include Rules # A contract includes more than method names. It also includes rules: Pop removes the same item that Peek would return. Count increases after Push and decreases after Pop . Pop and Peek on an empty stack are errors. A rule that must remain true for the object to be valid is called an invariant . Data-structure code often exists to preserve invariants while operations run quickly.

13.4.6. Iterators Are Lazy #

13.4.6. Iterators Are Lazy # An iterator method does not run its body when you call it — it runs one step at a time, only as far as the caller actually asks for elements. Calling EvenNumbers(1, 1000000) returns instantly; the loop body only executes as foreach requests each next value. This matters for two reasons: an iterator can describe an infinite or unbounded sequence without ever running forever, and a foreach that stops early (with break ) never computes the elements it never asked for.

24.2.1. Keep Connectivity State Separate from the Cable Budget #

24.2.1. Keep Connectivity State Separate from the Cable Budget # A minimum spanning forest connects every pair of vertices that can be connected by the input, without paying for unnecessary cycles. This is different from a shortest route from one office. Kruskal processes edges by nondecreasing cost, but “choose cheap edges” is incomplete: an edge is accepted only if its endpoints are in different current components. Union-find records those components. Each vertex starts as its own parent. Find(v) follows parent links to a root; equal roots mean already connected. Union(a,b) links the roots of two different components. Parent links here are

6.2.5. Keep Evidence After the Repair #

18.3.1. Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items #

18.3.1. Keep the Boundary of the Best K Items # A sales report needs the largest three amounts from a stream. Sorting every amount is one possible solution, but the requested result is smaller than the full sorted input. A min-heap of the currently retained best three exposes the weakest retained amount at its root. That is exactly the boundary a new candidate must beat. For amounts 7, 2, 9, 4, 10, retain 7, 2 and 9 first. Their minimum is 2. Candidate 4 replaces 2; candidate 10 replaces the new minimum 4. The retained values are 7, 9 and 10. Their heap storage need not be printed in sorted report order; sorting only the final retained values

19.2.6. Keys Must Keep Their Meaning #

19.2.6. Keys Must Keep Their Meaning # Do not change fields that determine a key’s equality or hash while that key is stored. The key can become inconsistent with its original bucket. Immutable string IDs avoid that mutation hazard. A custom business object may instead need a comparer based on an immutable ID, as introduced in Chapter 13. A hash collection does not provide sorted order, range queries, or next-priority removal. For those requirements choose another structure, or maintain multiple indexes with a clear consistency policy. The next section coordinates dictionary membership with the priority queue from Chapter 18.

Kruskal Invariants and the Cut Argument
  • Kruskal's algorithm; invariants and cut property
Replaced with the listed canonical subject terms at the preserved teaching locations.
24.2.5. Kruskal Invariants and the Cut Argument #

24.2.5. Kruskal Invariants and the Cut Argument # Accepted edges are acyclic. Union-find tracks exactly the components connected by accepted edges; an edge with equal roots would create a cycle. A minimum-cost crossing edge is safe: take the cut separating one current component from the rest. An optimal spanning forest that lacks the chosen edge can exchange a crossing edge on the resulting cycle for it without raising cost. Within each connected input component, this cut argument shows the accepted forest can be extended to an optimum. Acyclicity alone would not prove minimality. The implementation uses union by size and path halving. Sortin

8.2.4.6. Stacks and Queues # A stack follows last in, first out (LIFO) . Push adds an item at the top; Pop removes and returns the top item. Enqueue adds an item at the back; Dequeue removes and returns the item at the front. This expresses an arrival-order service line. Both collections below receive Order A followed by Order B . 17.4.3. Level Order with a Queue # Depth-first traversals finish descendants before moving to another branch. Level order visits nodes by depth: root first, then its children, then their children. Use the Chapter 15 queue as a worklist of nodes discovered but not yet processed. When you remove a node from the queue, append its existing children from left to right. The queue keeps earlier levels ahead of later ones. In a proper tree, each non-root node has exactly one parent, so it is enqueued once. 8.4.7. Dictionary Efficiency #

8.4.7. Dictionary Efficiency # You could simulate a Dictionary fairly easily by keeping a List of keys and a parallel List of values, in the same order. You would find the entry for a key with: int i = keys . IndexOf ( key ); return values [ i ]; Searching through a List this way takes time proportional to the length of the List — linear order . Through an implementation covered in data structures courses, a Dictionary instead uses a hash table , which makes the average lookup time constant order : roughly the same speed whether the dictionary holds ten entries or ten million. The correct two assignments are inserted.Next = node.Next; node.Next = inserted; . Reversing them makes inserted.Next refer to inserted itself. 14.2.9. A Complete Singly Linked Sequence #

14.2.9. A Complete Singly Linked Sequence # This wrapper presents the same Add , Insert , indexer, and RemoveAt operations as the dynamic array. Nodes are private so client code cannot accidentally create cycles or change count without updating the wrapper. NodeAt validates the index, then follows links. head! and Next! express facts established by the list invariants after validation; they do not create runtime null checks. If those invariants are broken, the suppression cannot repair them. Run the cell independently. It inserts the middle order, removes the head, empties the list, and appends again. 14.2.8. Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants #

14.2.8. Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants # To remove B after A, preserve B’s successor by setting A.Next = B.Next . Removing the first node instead requires head = head.Next , because there is no preceding node to update. Unlinking does not destroy the object immediately: other references might still reach it, and .NET manages reclamation of unreachable objects. A wrapper with a tail reference must maintain these rules: An empty list has count zero and both head and tail null. A nonempty list has a reachable head and tail, and tail.Next is null. 15.2.8. Linked Queue Endpoints and Growth Choices #

15.2.8. Linked Queue Endpoints and Growth Choices # A singly linked queue uses a head for removal and a tail for insertion. Empty means count zero and both endpoints null. A nonempty chain reaches tail last, and tail.Next is null. Removing the only node must clear tail as well as head; otherwise a later enqueue may attach to a detached node. Unlike removing the last item of a singly linked list, queue dequeue removes the head and needs no predecessor search. Each enqueue/dequeue performs a fixed number of link changes. The program still pays for allocation and memory management. Trace: Draw both endpoints for enqueue A, dequeue A, and enqueue

2.3.1.4. Logical Operators #

2.3.1.4. Logical Operators # Logical operators combine bool expressions to build compound conditions. C# evaluates them using short-circuit rules: for && , if the left side is false , the right side is skipped; for || , if the left side is true , the right side is skipped. This matters when the right side has side-effects or could throw an exception. Precedence: ! binds tightest, then && , then || . Use parentheses for clarity when mixing them: bool x = true , y = false ; x && y ; // false — both must be true x || y ; // true — at least one must be true ! x ; // false — inverts x

4. Iteration #

4. Iteration # Repeating a task is one of the most powerful things a program can do. This chapter covers fundamental loop structures in C#, especially for and while , and the patterns that make repetition correct and readable. Loop control : A loop needs a starting state, a continuation condition, and an update that moves it toward stopping. for loops : A for loop works well when the number of repetitions or index range is known. while loops : A while loop works well when repetition depends on a condition that may change during execution. Loop safety : Careful updates and stopping conditions prevent infinite loops and off-by-one errors. Loops

23.1.4. Lower and Upper Bounds for Duplicates # A lower bound is the first position with value ≥ target; an upper bound is the first position with value > target. Both can equal n. 1.3.2.3. Main: Where Execution Begins #

1.3.2.3. Main: Where Execution Begins # A method is a named block of code that performs a task. Main is this application’s entry point , the method .NET calls when the application starts. For now, recognize static void Main(string[] args) and put the executable statements inside its braces. void says this method returns no value; static lets it run without creating a Program object. args receives command-line arguments, which this application does not use. Methods, arrays, and objects receive their own treatment later.

14.3.9. Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation #

14.3.9. Memory and Locality Qualify the Recommendation # For int elements, the backing array places the integer values together. For reference-type elements, the reference slots are contiguous but their target objects need not be. Sequential array access often benefits from memory locality. A linked traversal follows separately allocated node objects, which may be scattered in memory. Linked lists also pay for a node object and link field per item. Dynamic arrays pay for spare capacity and occasional replacement arrays. Neither representation has universally smaller memory usage: the element type, spare capacity, object layout, and workload m

3.6.1. Resolve a Merge Conflict #

3.6.1. Resolve a Merge Conflict # A merge conflict asks you to decide how competing edits should be combined. Inspect the files reported by Git and read both versions around the conflict markers ( <<<<<<< , ======= , and >>>>>>> ). Edit each affected area into the intended final content, then remove the markers. Save the files, run the relevant program or tests, and review the diff. Stage the resolved files and follow Git’s instructions to complete the merge or commit. Do not leave conflict markers in source code, and do not choose a version merely to make the warning disappear.

24.2.4. MST Contracts and Disconnected Graphs #

24.2.4. MST Contracts and Disconnected Graphs # Kruskal uses undirected edges with explicit distinct vertices. Parallel edges are allowed; self-loops and unknown endpoints are rejected. Negative edge weights are valid for MSTs. If the graph is disconnected, return a minimum spanning forest and report component count; do not call it a spanning tree. 11.1.5. Mutable and Immutable Objects #

11.1.5. Mutable and Immutable Objects # An object is mutable when its observable state can change after construction. An immutable object keeps its observable state fixed. The Product below has read-only properties and no method that changes its fields. Its property values are strings and a decimal, so sharing it cannot later change the catalog values through a setter. Read-only access to a reference is not enough to make a whole object immutable. A read-only property could still return a mutable list or another mutable object. You must inspect what callers can reach through the public members. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Gene

1.3.5. Names, Keywords, and Case # An identifier names something in a program, such as Program or Main . C# is case-sensitive : Console , console , and CONSOLE are different spellings. Library names must match their declarations exactly, so use Console.WriteLine , including the capital C , W , and L . A keyword has a language-defined role. Reserved keywords , such as class , static , and void , are reserved for the language itself and cannot be ordinary identifiers. You have already seen them in the first console program; do not replace them with names of your own. Ordinary identifiers begin with a letter or underscore and can include digits

2.1.5. Naming Convention of Identifiers #

2.1.5. Naming Convention of Identifiers # Some of the common conventions [ 1 ] to follow when naming C# identifiers are: The characters must all be letters, digits, or underscores _ , and must start with a letter or underscore. C# is case sensitive: The identifiers name , NAME , and NaMe are different. By convention, C# programs use PascalCase for namespace, class, and method names and camelCase for variable and method parameters. [ 2 ] Use meaningful and descriptive names for variables, methods, and classes. Avoid keywords when naming identifiers (see Section 1.3 ).

3.2.8. Nested Conditionals #

3.2.8. Nested Conditionals # The problem-solving scenario that you want to model may require complex branching behavior by combining conditionals and, in particular, by nesting conditionals. Namely, we can create more complex branching behavior by nesting conditional blocks. When more than one condition needs to be true and one of the condition is the sub-condition of parent condition, nested if can be used. In other words, when we want to further test certain condition when a condition tested true.

1.1.5. Number Systems and Data Representation # A binary , or base-2, number uses the digits 0 and 1 . Each position has a value that is a power of two, just as decimal positions represent powers of ten. A byte contains eight bits, so it has 2^8 = 256 possible patterns, from 0000 0000 through 1111 1111 . The ASCII code for uppercase A is decimal 65. Its eight-bit representation is 0100 0001 . Work from right to left to convert the pattern: Bit position 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 Place value 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 Bit in 0100 0001 0 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 Only the 64 and 1 positions are set, so the value is 64 + 1 = 65 . One Contract, Multiple Representations # The same stack ADT can be represented in more than one way: Representation Main idea Array-backed stack Store items in contiguous slots and track the top index. List-backed stack Delegate storage growth to List<T> . Linked-node stack Store each item in a node that references the next node. If all three preserve the same contract, client code can use them through the same interface. This is representation independence .

13.2.7. Operation Costs #

13.2.7. Operation Costs # A data structure is not just correct or incorrect. It also has costs. Operation Array/List-backed stack Linked-node stack Push Usually O(1); occasional resize costs O(n) O(1) Pop O(1) O(1) Peek O(1) O(1) Random access by index O(1), if exposed O(n) Extra memory per item low one extra reference per node The best representation depends on the workload. If a program mostly pushes and pops at one end, either representation can work. If it needs fast index access, linked nodes are the wrong fit.

4.2.5. Step in loop header #

4.2.5. Step in loop header # i++ is a common pattern and it increments by 1. Most C# binary operations have a similar variation. For instance if op is + , - , * , / or % , variable op = expression means the same as variable = variable op expression For example x *= 5 ; is the same as x = x * 5 ;

21.2.2. Partial Correctness and Termination Are Separate Questions # An invariant helps establish what is true if execution reaches the exit. 7.2.2. Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements #

7.2.2. Passing an Array Does Not Copy Its Elements # A method parameter of type int[] receives a copy of the reference value. Caller and helper can therefore refer to the same array. This connects ordinary parameter passing from Chapter 5 with reference aliasing, without requiring pass-by-reference parameter syntax. State whether a processing helper may mutate its input. 2.2.2. Files, Folders, and Paths #

2.2.2. Files, Folders, and Paths # A directory , also called a folder, contains files and other directories. A path identifies their location. An absolute path begins at a filesystem root, such as C:\Users\Alex\workspace on Windows or /Users/alex/workspace on macOS. A relative path starts from the shell’s current working directory : the folder in which commands operate. . means the current directory; .. means its parent. Changing the working directory does not move the files. Put quotes around paths containing spaces, for example cd "course projects" .

9.5.1. Personal Data and the Law #

9.5.1. Personal Data and the Law # Privacy laws differ by place, but they share common ideas. Three examples: GDPR (EU Regulation 2016/679, applies from May 25, 2018) sets principles for processing personal data, including purpose limitation (use data only for the stated purpose), data minimisation (collect only what is needed), and storage limitation (do not keep it longer than needed). [ 1 ] CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act, in effect since January 1, 2020, and expanded by the CPRA from January 1, 2023) gives California residents rights to know about, delete, and opt out of the sale of their personal information. Preface #

Preface # This book teaches you to think like a computer scientist while you write real C# programs. It assumes no programming experience. The first course develops the skills to build a small multi-class information system that stores its data in a database. Further study introduces data structures and the algorithmic foundations needed to choose and use them. An optional algorithms sequence develops deeper analysis and problem-solving techniques. 4.4.5. Preview: Recursive GCD #

4.4.5. Preview: Recursive GCD # The first statement of Euclid’s algorithm said (in C#) when : gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b) It is saying the result of the function with one set of parameters is equal to calling the function with another set of parameters. If we put this into a C# function definition, it would mean the instructions for the function say to call itself . This is a broadly useful technique called recursion , where a function calls itself inside its definition. We don’t expect you to master this technique immediately but do feel that it is important you at least hear about it and see its tremendous power: /// Return the greatest commo

This avoids storing course names inside every student row.

18.1.1. Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array #

18.1.1. Priority Describes Removal, Not a Fully Sorted Array # A service desk chooses the lowest numbered priority next. That is a removal contract. It does not require that every stored element be maintained in complete sorted order, nor does it say that equal priorities must leave in arrival order. State the priority direction and tie policy before interpreting a printed storage array. A min-heap requires each parent’s priority to be no greater than its children’s. The root is therefore a minimum, but siblings need not be ordered. In the array [1, 4, 2, 7, 6, 3], the values 4 and 2 can appear in that order without violating the heap. Readin

Priority Is Different from Fairness
  • priority queue; fairness
Replaced with the listed canonical subject terms at the preserved teaching locations.
18.3.4. Priority Is Different from Fairness #

18.3.4. Priority Is Different from Fairness # A strict priority rule may postpone low-priority work indefinitely when urgent work keeps arriving. Stable arrival ties solve ordering among equal priorities, not fairness between priority levels. Choose a business rule for escalation or bounded urgent service before claiming a scheduler is fair. For top-k, state whether duplicates count as separate observations, what k=0 means, and how results are finally displayed. Maintaining a heap of at most k retained values costs O(k) storage and O(log k) repair per retained update; producing a sorted output is additional work.

8.2.4.7. Priority Queues #

8.2.4.7. Priority Queues # A priority queue chooses the next item using a priority value rather than its arrival position. In .NET’s default PriorityQueue<TElement,TPriority> , the item with the lowest priority value is removed first. A smaller number therefore means earlier processing in this example. This is a convention you must define for the application, not an automatic interpretation of what “high priority” means. [ 4 ] Each insertion supplies two pieces of information: the element to store and its priority. A routine request arrives first, but the urgent request leaves first because its priority value is smaller. 1 using System ; 2 us

8.2.4.5. Processing Order #

8.2.4.5. Processing Order # Sometimes the important question is which item should leave the collection next. A list lets you choose a position, but that freedom puts the responsibility for enforcing the processing rule on your program. A stack or queue expresses a particular rule through its operations. These structures do not decide an organization’s policy for you. If requests should be handled in arrival order, choose a collection that expresses that policy. If urgency should take precedence, make the urgency rule explicit and choose a different structure.

22.2.1. Prove the Combining Step Before Hiding It in Recursion # Assume two input runs are already sorted under the same policy. To merge them, compare their first unread elements and choose the smaller. No later element in either run can be smaller than that run’s first unread element, so the chosen value is safe as the next output. Recursion supplies sorted runs; it does not remove the need to justify this combining rule. Merge [2, 5] with [1, 5, 7]. Choose 1 from the right, then 2 from the left. At the tie between the two 5 values, choosing the left one first preserves relative order when these runs came from adjacent parts of the original

23.5.3. Quicksort #

23.5.3. Quicksort # Quicksort, also called partition sort, chooses a pivot and rearranges one subrange around it. The left scan skips values smaller than the pivot; the right scan skips larger values. When the scans stop before crossing, exchange the two values and advance both positions. Advancing after a swap is essential when values equal the pivot. The partition loop maintains these statements: everything before the left scan is at most the pivot, and everything after the right scan is at least the pivot. The unclassified interval shrinks. After the scans cross, recursively sort the remaining left and right subranges. They are not individ

Refactor Without Changing the Contract

Replaced with the listed canonical subject terms at the preserved teaching locations.
11.4.5. Refactor Without Changing the Contract #

11.4.5. Refactor Without Changing the Contract # Refactoring changes internal organization while preserving intended observable behavior. Suppose a console program keeps product names, prices, and quantities in parallel lists. Each insertion must update all three lists in the same order, so a missing update can silently pair the wrong price with a product. First capture a few expected orders as checks. Introduce Product and OrderLine , move line calculations into the line class, and move the line collection into Order . Keep the public task the same: add requested products and obtain the correct total. Run the checks after each small change.

14.2.6. References Are Paths, Not Copies #

14.2.6. References Are Paths, Not Copies # Work orders may also be represented by separate node objects. A node’s Next is a reference to another node, not an embedded copy of the remaining list. Assigning current = head copies a reference: both variables initially identify the same object. Changing current to current.Next moves a cursor without moving head . head ----> [WO-10 | next] ---> [WO-30 | null] current --^ If you traverse by repeatedly assigning to head , you lose your entry point to the sequence. 14.2.8. Removal, Head, and Tail Invariants # To remove B after A, preserve B’s successor by setting A.Next = B.Next . Removing the first node instead requires head = head.Next , because there is no preceding node to update. Unlinking does not destroy the object immediately: other references might still reach it, and .NET manages reclamation of unreachable objects. A wrapper with a tail reference must maintain these rules: An empty list has count zero and both head and tail null. A nonempty list has a reachable head and tail, and tail.Next is null. 18.2.1. Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb #

18.2.1. Repair Only the Part an Operation Can Disturb # Enqueue adds a new entry at the next open leaf position so the complete shape is preserved. All old parent-child relations are unchanged. Only the new entry’s path toward the root can violate min-heap order. Bubble-up compares with the parent and swaps while the child is smaller. Moving upward strictly decreases its index, so repair terminates. Start with [2, 5, 4] and enqueue 1. Appending produces [2, 5, 4, 1]. Comparing 1 with parent 5 gives [2, 1, 4, 5]. Comparing that 1 with root 2 gives [1, 2, 4, 5]. Do not sort the whole array; that would enforce a stronger and more expensive condi

23.1.5. Repeated-Query Workloads #

23.1.5. Repeated-Query Workloads # For q lookups, scanning costs up to Θ(qn). Sorting once and searching costs Θ(n log n+q log n), assuming a comparison sort and static data. Updates can invalidate the sorted snapshot or require maintenance. Sorting merely to answer one query may add work; an existing sorted array can support binary search even for one query. Dictionary exact-key lookup needs its own duplicate and update policy; ordered ranges and all matches are different requirements.

One Contract, Multiple Representations # The same stack ADT can be represented in more than one way: Representation Main idea Array-backed stack Store items in contiguous slots and track the top index. List-backed stack Delegate storage growth to List<T> . Linked-node stack Store each item in a node that references the next node. If all three preserve the same contract, client code can use them through the same interface. This is representation independence .

26.2.1. Build the Fallback Table Before Scanning Text # KMP avoids restarting a search from scratch after every mismatch. It retains a fact already proved: a suffix of the consumed text matches a prefix of the pattern. This connects direct matching’s result contract to a different reuse rule. The goal remains all overlapping ordinal matches; changing the algorithm must not change that answer. For each pattern position i, prefix[i] records the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also its suffix. Proper excludes the entire segment. The number is a length, not an index of the next text character. For ABABACA, complete the table from l

26.2.3. Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix #

26.2.3. Reuse a Prefix Only When It Is Also the Needed Suffix # KMP remembers how much of a pattern has already matched. After a mismatch, some of that matched text may also be a valid beginning of the next candidate match. The prefix table identifies such borders: proper prefixes that are also suffixes. Proper excludes the complete string itself, otherwise fallback would make no progress. For pattern ABAB, the longest proper border of the whole pattern is AB, length two. 2.2.1.4. Type Conversion # C# variables have specific types, but values sometimes need to move between types. Type conversions are either implicit (automatic) or explicit (manual cast required). Implicit casting happens automatically when converting a smaller type to a larger one — no data is lost: char → int → long → float → double Explicit casting is required when converting a larger type to a smaller one, because precision or range may be lost: double → float → long → int → char For example: int a = 123 ; long b = a ; // implicit: int fits in long, no cast needed int c = ( int ) b ; // explicit: long → int, cast required Use GetType() to i

25.1.1. Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule #

25.1.1. Compare Three Executions of the Same Dependency Rule # A repeated subproblem is a question with the same complete state, not just a similarly named function call. With F(0)=0, F(1)=1 and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2), the integer n fully identifies the question. Fix that definition before sharing results. Changing the base values creates a different sequence and invalidates an old cache. For F(4), the naive call tree asks for F(3) and F(2). F(3) asks for F(2) and F(1), so F(2) is expanded twice. Termination is already guaranteed by decreasing n; the problem is repeated work. F(4) F(3) F(2) F(1) F(0) F(1) F(2) F(1)

Computing F(5) asks for F(4) and F(3); computing F(4) asks for F(3) again. A cache can retain the completed answer for a numeric argument and reuse it when that same subproblem returns. The key is sufficient because the recurrence and base cases are fixed for this computation. Memoization starts from the requested state and recursively solves missing dependencies. 5.1.1.4. A Small Schema # A schema is the planned structure of a database. Here is a small bookstore schema: CREATE TABLE Books ( BookId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , Title TEXT NOT NULL , Author TEXT NOT NULL , Price REAL NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE Sales ( SaleId INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , BookId INTEGER NOT NULL , Quantity INTEGER NOT NULL , SoldOn TEXT NOT NULL , FOREIGN KEY ( BookId ) REFERENCES Books ( BookId ) ); Books stores facts about each book. Sales stores events that happened over time. The foreign key tells us which book each sale refers to.

5.2.8. Scope #

5.2.8. Scope # A variable declared inside a method definition is called a local variable . This declaration may be in either the parameter list or in the body of the method. A local variable comes into existence after the method is called, and ceases to exist after that method call terminates. In these noncapturing examples, a local name is visible only in its containing scope, and each call has separate local values. Scope and lifetime are different concepts; nested scopes and later captured-variable examples require more precise rules. Its value may be transferred outside of the method scope by standard means, principally: If it is the expr

23.1.5. Repeated-Query Workloads # For q lookups, scanning costs up to Θ(qn). Sorting once and searching costs Θ(n log n+q log n), assuming a comparison sort and static data. Updates can invalidate the sorted snapshot or require maintenance. Sorting merely to answer one query may add work; an existing sorted array can support binary search even for one query. Dictionary exact-key lookup needs its own duplicate and update policy; ordered ranges and all matches are different requirements.

19.1.4. Separate Chaining and Complete Operations # A collision occurs when different keys choose the same bucket. Separate chaining stores a collection of entries at each bucket. A lookup computes the bucket and compares keys within that chain. An update must search the chain before appending; otherwise it can create duplicate keys. Removal must preserve the other colliding entries. With four buckets, IDs 101, 105, and 109 all choose bucket one. To find 109, inspect 101, then 105, then 109. To report that 113 is absent, inspect the entire chain. A successful lookup may stop early; an unsuccessful one must establish that no matching key exist

23.4.2. Shell Sort #

23.4.2. Shell Sort # Shell sort applies insertion sorting to subsequences whose elements are separated by a gap. For gap four, the sequences start at positions zero, one, two, and three, visiting every fourth element. A distant exchange can remove several inversions, moving an out-of-place value toward its destination more quickly than adjacent exchanges alone. A single gap does not necessarily sort the whole array. Repeat with decreasing gaps, ending at one; the final pass is ordinary insertion sort over the entire array. After a gap-four pass, each gap-four subsequence is sorted, but neighboring values can still be out of order. Trace this

23.4.1. Each Gap Pass Solves an Interleaved Insertion Problem # Shell sort connects to insertion sort by ordering positions separated by a chosen gap. With gap three, positions zero, three, six form one subsequence; positions one, four, seven form another. A pass applies insertion-like work within each subsequence. It does not claim the whole array is already sorted after that pass. As gaps shrink, long-distance disorder can be reduced before the final gap-one insertion pass. 15.1.1. Stack Behavior #

15.1.1. Stack Behavior # A stack is an abstract data type where the most recently added item is the next item removed. This access rule is called last in, first out , or LIFO . The core operations are small: Push(value) adds a value to the top. Pop() removes and returns the top value. Peek() returns the top value without removing it. Count reports how many values are currently stored. The point of a stack is not that it stores data in a new magical way. The point is that it restricts access so the program can only work with the top item. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Generic ; 3 4 var undoHistory = new Stack < string > (); 5 und

8.2.4.6. Stacks and Queues #

8.2.4.6. Stacks and Queues # A stack follows last in, first out (LIFO) . Push adds an item at the top; Pop removes and returns the top item. Think of an undo history: the most recent action should normally be the first action undone. Storing a description of an action is only a demonstration of ordering; a real undo feature also needs a way to reverse that action. A queue follows first in, first out (FIFO) . Enqueue adds an item at the back; Dequeue removes and returns the item at the front. This expresses an arrival-order service line. Both collections below receive Order A followed by Order B . 5.2.3. Static Variables # You may define static variables (variables defined with the word static inside the class, but outside of any method definition). These variables are visible inside all of your methods in the class. Instead of local scope, static variables have class scope .
