5.2.3. Static Variables #

5.2.3. Static Variables # You may define static variables (variables defined with the word static inside the class, but outside of any method definition). These variables are visible inside all of your methods in the class. Instead of local scope, static variables have class scope . It is good programming practice generally to avoid defining static variables and instead to put your variables inside methods and explicitly pass them as parameters where needed. A fixed value shared by the class can be a constant. A const field is implicitly static; a mutable static field is not a constant. For example, A constant is a name that you give a fixed

5.2.9. Static Storage Reference #

5.2.9. Static Storage Reference # There may be a declaration prefaced by the word static that appears inside a class and outside of any method definition in the class. Static variables are visible within each method of the class, and may be used by the methods. A const field gives a name to a fixed compile-time value and is implicitly static. Mutable static fields instead hold shared state; do not confuse the two. Footnotes

4.2.5. Step in loop header #

4.2.5. Step in loop header # i++ is a common pattern and it increments by 1. Also common in the iterator/step section of the loop header is using assignment statement to control stepping: 1 int i = 10 ; 2 int k = 10 ; 3 i = i + k ; or the equivalent short-hand compound assignment operator: 1 int i = 10 ; 2 int k = 10 ; 3 i += k ; This means to increment the variable i by k. Most C# binary operations have a similar variation. For instance if op is + , - , * , / or % , variable op = expression means the same as variable = variable op expression For example x *= 5 ; is the same as x = x * 5 ;

Most C# binary operations have a similar variation. For instance if op is + , - , * , / or % , variable op = expression means the same as variable = variable op expression For example x *= 5 ; is the same as x = x * 5 ;

2.4.5. String Interpolation # The $ character identifies a string literal as an interpolated string . An interpolated string is a string literal that might contain interpolation expressions. When an interpolated string is resolved to a result string, the compiler replaces items with interpolation expressions by the string representations of the expression results. String interpolation provides a more readable, convenient syntax to format strings. To identify a string literal as an interpolated string, prepend it with the $ symbol. Compare composite formatting and string interpolation : 1 var name = "Mark" ; 2 var date = DateTime . Now ; 3 4 /

Increment i so the next iteration adds the next number. Start sum = 0 and i = 1 so zero terms also work. Continue while i <= n . 3.2.14. The break Keyword #

3.2.14. The break Keyword # break exits the switch after the selected case. The program then continues with the statement after the switch. C# does not allow ordinary execution to fall through from a nonempty case into the next case. Several case labels can share one body, but simply removing break from a nonempty body is not valid. Use braces around decision bodies to make their boundaries clear. A semicolon immediately after if (condition) creates an empty statement and can make following code execute unconditionally. The While-Statements example explains that pitfall. Footnotes [ 1 ] Further reading: Nakov and colleagues, Conditional State

6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question #

6.4.3. Thinking Through an Ethical Question # Ethical decisions in software are rarely about villains. They are usually about trade-offs under deadline pressure. A short checklist keeps the important questions from being skipped: Who is affected? List the stakeholders: users, customers, coworkers, the organization, and people outside it. What could happen, and how bad would it be? Consider likely and severe outcomes for each stakeholder. What do we owe them? Consider laws, contracts, promises made to customers, and professional codes. Could we explain this decision publicly? If a decision only works while nobody knows about it, reconsider it.

16.1.2. Trace a Shrinking Candidate Region # For a half-open interval [lo, hi), every candidate is at least lo and strictly before hi. Empty means lo equals hi. A midpoint comparison removes a region that cannot contain the desired result under the contract. The important progress argument is that every continuing iteration strictly shrinks the candidate region. Merely changing lo or hi is not enough if an update can leave the same interval. A common off-by-one mistake mixes an inclusive upper bound with a loop intended for half-open intervals. 21.3.2. Track Rounding and Live Storage # For odd n, two subproblems cannot both have size n/2 as an integer. A range split may have floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2) items. Together they must still cover the whole input without overlap or omission. Bounds can simplify rounding when justified, but an implementation must handle exact endpoints. In a balanced two-child recursion, a level can contain many calls even though only one root-to-leaf path is active at a time in depth-first execution. 5.2.5. Transactions for Related Changes #

5.2.5. Transactions for Related Changes # The optional Sell operation begins a transaction, reduces stock only if enough remains, inserts a sale, and commits. If the book is missing or stock is insufficient, it rolls back and returns false . If an unexpected error occurs before commit, disposal rolls back the uncommitted transaction. Every command participating in the transaction sets its Transaction property. Updating stock and inserting the sale independently could leave only one change saved after a failure. Atomicity means these changes are committed together.

Traversal and Shared References # Traversal , also called enumeration , means visiting a collection’s elements. foreach provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. PriorityQueue is a special case: it exposes an UnorderedItems view for enumeration instead of supporting foreach directly on the queue. 8.2.5. Traversal and Shared References # Traversal , also called enumeration , means visiting a collection’s elements. foreach provides familiar syntax for this work, but the order and the kind of element you receive depend on the collection. Arrays and lists follow their sequence order. A dictionary enumerates key/value entries. A set supports enumeration, but its purpose is membership rather than sorted traversal. PriorityQueue is a special case: it exposes an UnorderedItems view for enumeration instead of supporting foreach directly on the queue. That view does not promise priority order; use successive removals when you need that order. T

17.3.7. Tree Shape and Library Choice #

17.3.7. Tree Shape and Library Choice # Inserting already sorted keys into a plain binary search tree can create a chain. Its height becomes n-1 edges, so a lookup can take O(n) comparisons. Balanced search trees maintain a height proportional to log n by restructuring after updates; learning the tradeoff does not require implementing rotations in this foundation course. Choose SortedSet for unique ordered values or SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> for ordered key/value reports. Choose a hash collection when exact-key membership matters and sorted iteration is unnecessary. Measure the workload and check the contract rather than assuming every ty

17.4.3. Level Order with a Queue #

17.4.3. Level Order with a Queue # Depth-first traversals finish descendants before moving to another branch. Level order visits nodes by depth: root first, then its children, then their children. Use the Chapter 15 queue as a worklist of nodes discovered but not yet processed. When you remove a node from the queue, append its existing children from left to right. The queue keeps earlier levels ahead of later ones. In a proper tree, each non-root node has exactly one parent, so it is enqueued once. Graphs with shared descendants or cycles need an additional visited set, a topic for Chapter 20. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Gener

6.2.1. Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence #

6.2.1. Debug One Familiar Loop from Symptom to Evidence # Before the retained array and CSV applications, use a calculation that needs only methods, decisions, and loops. A shop awards one credit for each of the first days days. With three days, the expected credits are 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. This expectation comes from the problem, not from running the implementation. The following complete cell deliberately contains a logic defect. It compiles, but the loop stops too soon. A compiler cannot infer that the business rule requires the last day. 1 using System ; 2 static int Credits ( int days ) 3 { 4 int total = 0 ; 5 for ( int day = 1 ; day < days ;

6.2.3. Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question #

6.2.3. Turn a Symptom into a Reproducible Question # A report says that three expense entries, 12, 8 and 5, total 20. Saying that the total is wrong identifies a symptom, but it does not yet locate the defect. First derive the expected total independently: 12 + 8 + 5 is 25. Keep the three inputs fixed. A changing input set makes it difficult to tell whether a code change repaired the problem or merely avoided it. Suppose the program loops while index is less than the number of entries minus one. The loop body may contain correct addition and still omit the final item. This is why debugging begins with the contract and a concrete failing case

3.5.1. Work on More Than One Computer # GitHub also lets you move between a lab computer and your own. The remote copy is the meeting point, so each session follows the same cycle: Start: run git pull --ff-only to bring down changes you pushed from another computer. Work: create or change files, then run and check your program. Record: run git add for the files you intend to include, then git commit -m "message" . Finish: run git push before you leave, so the work is on GitHub. If you forget the last step, your work stays on the first computer. Push at the end of every session. 2.2.1.4. Type Conversion #

2.2.1.4. Type Conversion # C# variables have specific types, but values sometimes need to move between types. Type conversions are either implicit (automatic) or explicit (manual cast required). Implicit casting happens automatically when converting a smaller type to a larger one — no data is lost: char → int → long → float → double Explicit casting is required when converting a larger type to a smaller one, because precision or range may be lost: double → float → long → int → char For example: int a = 123 ; long b = a ; // implicit: int fits in long, no cast needed int c = ( int ) b ; // explicit: long → int, cast required Use GetType() to i

2.2.1. Types # In C#, everything is a type . Every value you store, every variable you declare, and every expression you write has a type. A type defines three things: Value : The set of valid values it can hold (e.g., int holds whole numbers −2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647). Operation : The operations permitted on those values (e.g., arithmetic on numbers, .Length on strings). Memory : The amount of memory reserved when a variable of that type is created. 19.2.4. Union, Intersection, and Difference # Let registered contain everyone registered for a workshop and attended contain everyone who checked in. Their intersection contains registered attendees. Registered minus attended identifies no-shows. Attended minus registered identifies walk-ins. Their union contains everyone appearing in either source. HashSet operations such as IntersectWith and ExceptWith mutate the receiving set. Construct a copy first when you need to retain both source sets. 2.2.1.1.5. A Note on Unmanaged Types # C#’s reference documentation also names a category called unmanaged types — value types whose fields, all the way down, are themselves value types with no references anywhere inside them ( int , a struct made only of int fields, and so on). The category exists because a small set of advanced features — interop with native code, and low-level performance-sensitive code using pointers — are restricted to types that satisfy this guarantee. You do not need to identify unmanaged types yourself in this book; it is mentioned here only so the term is not a surprise if you encounter it in official C# documentatio

26.1.3. Use Mismatches as Evidence # A mismatch at one candidate start establishes only that this candidate fails. It does not prove that the text contains no later occurrence. The outer loop advances the start; the inner loop advances the pattern position. Confusing those two positions can skip starts or compare the wrong slices. With text length n and pattern length m, a direct comparison model can perform up to proportional to n*m work for nonempty patterns within the text. 2.2.1.1.1. Value Types # A variable of a value type directly contains its data. Value types include the numeric primitives ( int , double , long , and the rest), bool , char , and user-defined struct and enum types. Despite their keyword status, each built-in value type is simply an alias for a .NET struct in the System namespace — int is System.Int32 , bool is System.Boolean . [ 2 ] Assigning one value-type variable to another copies the value . 5.2.2. Variable Scopes #

5.2.2. Variable Scopes # A variable may be available for use in some parts of code, but not others. The scope of a variable is the region of the program that the variable is visible, which means it is accessible by name and can be used in the part of code. C# scope rules of variables can be divided into three categories as follows: Class Level Scope Method Level Scope Block Level Scope. A variable declared inside a method is a local variable . A body local belongs to its containing block; a parameter is available in the method body. A nested-block local cannot be used outside that block. You cannot use a local variable before its declaration

3.1. Why Use Version Control #

3.1. Why Use Version Control # Version control gives you a record of your work that you can inspect, undo, and share. It helps individuals as much as teams: you can see what changed and when, return to a working version, and keep a copy off your own computer. It also replaces carrying files on USB drives or sending e-mail attachments, because you and your instructor can look at the same repository. The basic idea is to keep a main copy of a project on GitHub (the remote ) and a working copy on each computer you use (the local repository). 2.2.1.1.3. void # void is a special case: it means “no type,” used only as a method’s return type to say the method does not return a value. You cannot declare a variable of type void — void x; is a compile-time error, because void describes an absence of a value, not a kind of value. You will use it constantly starting in Chapter 5, whenever a method’s job is to do something (print output, modify state) rather than compute and return a result: For now, recognize this distinction in built-in calls: Math.Abs(-3) produces a value that can be stored, while Console.WriteLine("Hello") prints a message and produces no result to assign. 6.4. Validate a Supplied Walk #

6.4. Validate a Supplied Walk # A walk checker receives a route chosen elsewhere. It does not discover a route or prove optimality. Validate each label and each consecutive edge, then sum the weights. A repeated vertex is legal for a walk, so a return trip contributes its edges again. Use a long total to accumulate integer weights without overflowing an int on a long route. Return false for an empty route, an unknown vertex, or a missing direct edge. A known singleton route succeeds with cost zero. On failure, leave the output at zero rather than returning a partial trip cost. 1 using System ; 2 using System.Collections.Generic ; 3 using Syst

20.1.5. Walks, Paths, and Cycles #

20.1.5. Walks, Paths, and Cycles # A walk is a sequence in which each consecutive pair is joined by an edge in the required direction. A walk may repeat vertices and edges. A path in this chapter is a walk without repeated vertices. A cycle is a closed walk with no repeated edges or vertices except its start/end. 13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies #

13.1.3. What an ADT Specifies # An ADT describes a set of values and the operations allowed on those values. It does not require one particular internal representation. For a stack, the contract might say: Operation Meaning Push(item) Add an item to the top. Pop() Remove and return the top item. Peek() Return the top item without removing it. Count Report how many items are stored. This contract says nothing about arrays or linked lists. That separation is the point: client code should depend on the behavior it needs, not on accidental implementation details.

14.1.9. Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost #

14.1.9. Why Doubling Gives Amortized Constant Cost # For nine appends, the trace copies 2 + 4 + 8 = 14 existing entries and writes nine new entries. Counting these array writes gives 23 writes across nine operations. Some individual appends are costly, but the total grows in proportion to the number of appends. For a longer sequence, copy sizes form 2 + 4 + 8 + ... . Each term is twice the previous one, so the sum stays below twice the final number of inserted items. Adding one write per appended item still gives a total proportional to n . Dividing total work by n gives a constant amortized cost. This is a bound over an operation sequence, n

Writing an Iterator with yield return # Implementing IEnumerator<T> by hand — tracking a position field, writing MoveNext() and Current yourself — is tedious for something as simple as “count from one number to another.” The yield return statement lets the compiler generate that machinery for you. 2.4.3. Output #

2.4.3. Output # In a regular C# program, including the VS Code projects used in this book, values are not displayed just because an expression exists in the source code. You must explicitly give the program an instruction to print to the console or terminal. This printing is accomplished through a method with a long name: Console.WriteLine . Like with math, you can pass a method a value to work on, by placing it in parentheses after the name of the method. Console is a C# class maintained by the system, that interacts with the terminal or console window where text output appears for the program. A method defined in that class is WriteLine . T
